title: Amortized Analysis: When One Slow Step Is Fine
oneLiner: Why appending to a list is O(1) even though some appends copy everything, and why a while inside a for is often still O(n).
keyTakeaway: Amortized analysis bounds the TOTAL cost of a sequence of operations, then divides by the count. If every element can only be pushed once and popped once, or a pointer can only move forward, count those moves over the whole run instead of multiplying the loop bounds.
explanation:
Worst case per operation can be misleading. A dynamic array (C# List<T>, Python list) has spare capacity; when it runs out, it allocates a bigger array and copies every element, which costs O(n) for that one append. But because it grows by a constant FACTOR, the expensive appends get exponentially rarer: copying 4, then 8, then 16 items, up to n, adds up to less than 2n. So n appends cost O(n) in total, and we say each append is amortized O(1). Grow by a constant AMOUNT instead and the copies add up to O(n²). Hash tables use the same trick when they resize.

Amortized is not the same as average case. Average case is about random inputs (a hash lookup is O(1) on average over hash values). Amortized is a guarantee over any sequence of operations: no input can make n appends cost more than O(n). Interviewers like hearing that distinction.

The same counting argument explains loops that look nested but are linear. In a sliding window, the right pointer moves n times and the left pointer can only move forward, so it moves at most n times in total, however the while loop is written. In a monotonic stack, each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the inner while loop pops at most n times over the whole run. A queue built from two stacks moves each element between stacks once. In all of these the right question is not "how many times can the inner loop run per outer trip" but "how many times can it run in total".
